name: Cabbage leaf diet

lead: The cabbage leaf diet is a fad diet in which cabbage, usually as a soup, is eaten heavily for about a week. People use it for quick weight loss, hoping to look slimmer in the face and midsection.
It is typically promoted as a way to lose about 10 pounds (4.5 kg) in a week. Dietitians cited by Wikipedia say most of that is water, so it is not permanent.

paras: Most versions let followers eat as much cabbage soup as they want during the week, supplemented with other foods on a daily schedule. It is a short fixed-length plan rather than a long-term diet.
Reported side effects include dehydration, headaches, dizziness, nausea, fatigue, gas, bloating, muscle loss and nutrient deficiencies. Calorie intake is far below what is considered safe long-term.

Leaner, less bloated appearance short term
angle.text: People use it for a quick drop in scale weight before an event. Dietitians report that most of the early loss is water.

lead: The cabbage leaf diet is a variation of the cabbage soup diet, a seven-day plan in which a low-calorie cabbage soup is eaten heavily.[1] People turn to it for rapid weight loss, which can mean a leaner face and body.

Its origins are unknown but date to the 1950s; it spread in the 1980s by fax and carries names such as the "Sacred Heart Diet" and "Military Cabbage Soup", though the named institutions have denied any connection.[1]
Fad diets of this kind are popular online; a Google Trends analysis ranked diet popularity globally from 2004 to 2019.[2] No clinical trials of the cabbage soup diet are listed.

paras: Most versions allow unlimited cabbage soup during the week.[1]
The plan dates to the 1950s and spread widely in the 1980s as "faxlore". Hospitals and the military named in its labels have denied any link.[1]

Experts note that losing that much body fat in a week is nearly impossible, that most reported loss is water and so not lasting, and that the calorie intake is below what is considered safe long-term. Reported side effects include dehydration, dizziness, muscle loss and nutrient deficiencies.[1]
No studies found. A Google Trends analysis examined diet popularity but did not test this diet.[2]
